mcq.q: Decode at small batch is usually limited by…
mcq.why: Each step reads all weights for little arithmetic, so bandwidth dominates.

mcq.q: Why is prefill compute-bound?
options: All prompt tokens are processed in one parallel pass, with lots of maths per weight read
It reads weights once per token
mcq.why: Many tokens share each weight read, so the GPU runs near its FLOP limit.

mcq.q: What makes up time to first token (TTFT)?
mcq.why: TTFT grows with prompt length.
distractors: Network is only part of it.
Decode comes after the first token.
That is the rest of the response.

mcq.q: Using the figure's rates (prefill 10,000 tokens/s, decode 60 tokens/s), what is TTFT for a 20,000-token prompt with no queue?
End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × ITL. With TTFT 0.5 s, 301 output tokens and ITL 20 ms, what is it?
Long prompts mostly hurt ___; long outputs mostly hurt ___.
mcq.why: Prompts are prefilled before the first token; outputs are decoded after it.
distractors: ITL barely changes with prompt length.

mcq.q: Why does batching help decode throughput?
options: It makes each token cheaper to compute alone
Many sequences share each weight read
mcq.why: Decode is bandwidth-bound; batching amortises the read.

mcq.q: In the laptop lab, why is the second TTFT lower when you rerun the same prompt?
options: Ollama reuses the cached prompt prefix
The CPU warmed up the disk
mcq.why: Prefix caching skips prefill for the repeated part (14.3).

mcq.q: Why is dividing total tokens by total time a poor metric for a chat service?
options: It hides whether the wait was before or during generation
mcq.why: Users perceive TTFT and ITL separately.

mcq.q: Which do chat users perceive most?
mcq.why: Chat users notice the wait before text appears; batch jobs care about total time.

interview.q: Explain prefill and decode and what limits each.
covers: decode one token per step, bandwidth-bound

mcq.q: What does paged attention mainly fix?
mcq.why: Fixed-size blocks allocated on demand avoid reserving max-length contiguous memory.

mcq.q: What is the main problem with static batching?
options: Short requests wait for the longest one, and new arrivals wait for the whole batch
mcq.why: Slots sit idle while the longest request finishes.

mcq.q: What does continuous batching do?
options: Re-forms the batch every decode step: finished sequences leave and waiting ones join
Runs one request at a time
mcq.why: This typically multiplies throughput several-fold.

mcq.q: What is chunked prefill for?
options: Splitting a new request's prefill so it does not stall decoding of others
mcq.why: Long prefills are inserted in pieces between decode steps.

mcq.q: How does paged attention store the KV cache?
options: In one contiguous max-length buffer per sequence
In fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and mapped by a per-sequence block table
mcq.why: Like virtual memory pages; blocks can be shared.
distractors: That is the waste it fixes.

mcq.q: A bot sends a 6,000-token shared prefix and 800 unique tokens per request. On a prefix-cache hit, how many tokens need prefill?
mcq.why: Only the unique part is prefilled on a hit.
distractors: The unique tokens still need prefill.

mcq.q: Input price $3 per million tokens, 90% cached-token discount. On a hit, what is the input cost of 6,000 cached plus 800 new tokens?
distractors: That leaves out the cached tokens.
That leaves out the new tokens.
That is a miss at full price.

mcq.q: How should prompts be structured to benefit from prefix caching?
options: Stable content first (system prompt, tools), dynamic content after
mcq.why: The cache matches from the start of the prompt (7.2).

mcq.q: Does prefix caching reduce decode cost?
options: No; it skips part of prefill only
mcq.why: Decode still runs for every output token.

mcq.q: Is sharing prefix-cache blocks across tenants automatically safe?
options: No; decide what may be shared and keep tenant-specific text isolated
Yes, if the model is the same
mcq.why: Shared caches can leak information through timing or content if not designed carefully.
distractors: Same model does not mean same trust.

mcq.q: A 70B model on 4 GPUs with TP=4 is how many serving units for redundancy?
mcq.why: The tensor-parallel group serves as one unit; losing any GPU stops it.

mcq.q: What does tensor parallelism split?
options: Each layer's matrices across GPUs in one node
mcq.why: TP communicates every layer, usually over NVLink.

mcq.q: What is the main way to scale throughput?
options: Data parallelism: independent replicas behind a load balancer
mcq.why: Replicas add capacity; TP is for fit and latency.
distractors: TP mainly helps fit and per-token latency.

mcq.q: What does prefix-aware routing do?
options: Sends requests with the same prefix to the same replica to hit its cache
Sends requests to the least loaded GPU only
mcq.why: Each replica's prefix cache is local.

mcq.q: What is disaggregated serving?
options: Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools, transferring the KV cache
Running each layer on a different node
mcq.why: Each pool can be sized for its workload.

mcq.q: A 70B FP8 model needs about how much memory for weights?
600 concurrent 4k-token conversations need about 790 GB of KV. Each TP=4 unit has about 215 GB for KV. About how many units are needed before headroom?
Plan redundancy for a model served as TP=4 units. How?
mcq.why: Losing any GPU stops its whole unit.
distractors: A spare GPU cannot replace a whole unit instantly.

mcq.q: Which parallelism uses all-to-all communication to route tokens?
mcq.why: MoE tokens are sent to their experts on other GPUs.
distractors: Replicas do not communicate per token.

mcq.q: Harbor runs its 70B model as two TP=4 units. One GPU fails. What remains?
options: Seven GPUs serving as seven units
mcq.why: The failed GPU takes its whole unit out.
distractors: GPUs in a TP group are not independent servers.

mcq.q: KV cache bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value. For 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and BF16, what is it?
distractors: That is FP8 (1 byte per value).

mcq.q: What usually limits how many users one GPU can serve?
mcq.why: KV cache grows with context × concurrent sequences.

mcq.q: How does grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads) change the KV cache?
mcq.why: Each KV head is shared by 4 query heads.
distractors: Fewer KV heads means less cache.
Keys and values are still cached.

mcq.q: An 8B model in BF16 on an 80 GB GPU leaves about 56 GB for KV. At 128 KiB per token, about how many 8k-token conversations fit?
distractors: That is the count at 128k context.

mcq.q: What does switching the KV cache from BF16 to FP8 do?
options: Removes the need for overhead memory
mcq.why: One byte per value instead of two.

mcq.q: How do serving engines typically allocate memory for the KV cache?
options: Allocate per request from scratch with no reserve
Reserve a fraction (e.g. 90%) of GPU memory and use what remains after weights
mcq.why: The KV pool is what is left after weights and overhead.

mcq.q: A team plans for a 128k context at 32 concurrent users on an 8B model. What does the estimator show?
options: It fits on one 24 GB GPU
The KV cache alone needs about 540 GB
Context length does not affect memory
mcq.why: KV grows linearly with context × users.

mcq.q: Choose all the components of GPU memory at inference.
mcq.why: Optimiser state is for training only.

mcq.q: Weights for an 8B model in FP8 take about…
mcq.why: 8 × 10⁹ parameters × 1 byte.

mcq.q: Why do providers price long context higher or cap concurrency?
options: Long prompts are harder to tokenise
Long context needs a new model
KV cache memory grows with context length and concurrent sequences
mcq.why: That arithmetic drives context pricing and concurrency limits.

mcq.q: Why does quantising weights speed up decode?
options: Fewer bytes are read per token
mcq.why: Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.

mcq.q: Which capabilities often degrade first under aggressive quantisation?
mcq.why: Always evaluate on your task suite.

mcq.q: How should you judge a quantised model?
options: On your own task suite, not just perplexity
mcq.why: Perplexity can hide task-specific losses.

mcq.q: Speculative decoding with acceptance rate a = 0.5 and k = 4 draft tokens: expected tokens per target pass = (1 − a^(k+1)) / (1 − a). What is it?
distractors: Too low; the target always adds one token.
That assumes every draft is accepted.

mcq.q: Does speculative decoding change the output distribution?
options: No; it is mathematically the same as the target model's
Yes, it is always lower quality
Yes, it follows the draft model
mcq.why: The target verifies drafts and accepts only the correct prefix.

mcq.q: When does speculative decoding help most?
options: High acceptance (predictable text, code) and small batch sizes
mcq.why: At large batches the GPU is already busy.

mcq.q: Does a 4-bit model always have lower latency than FP8?
options: No; it depends on kernel support, hardware and batch size
mcq.why: A format without fast kernels can be slower.

mcq.q: Why is a 4-bit 8B model about 4.5–5 GB rather than exactly 4 GB?
options: Scales and other tensors add more than 0.5 bytes per parameter
mcq.why: Quantisation scales and unquantised layers add overhead.

mcq.q: Choose all the compression methods besides quantisation that the chapter lists.
mcq.why: Adding layers makes models bigger.

mcq.q: An 8B model's weights shrink from 16 GB (BF16) to 8 GB (FP8). The chapter's table shows decode speed of about 1.6–1.9×, not 2×. Why?
options: Dequantisation work and non-weight memory traffic (such as the KV cache) do not shrink
FP8 is computed on the CPU
mcq.why: Speedups are below the ideal byte ratio.

mcq.q: Which engine is described as the default open-source GPU serving engine?
mcq.why: PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching and an OpenAI-compatible server.
distractors: Aimed at CPUs, Apple silicon and consumer GPUs.

mcq.q: What is TGI's status according to the chapter?
options: In maintenance mode; Hugging Face recommends vLLM or SGLang for new deployments
mcq.why: Check its README for the current status.

mcq.q: Choose all the parts of a cold start.
options: Pulling the image and loading weights
Allocating KV cache and compiling CUDA graphs
mcq.why: Together these can take several minutes.

mcq.q: Why is GPU utilisation a poor autoscaling signal?
options: It is too expensive to read
It lags and does not show waiting work; queue depth, KV usage and TTFT are better
mcq.why: Leading signals react before users wait.

mcq.q: When should a replica be marked ready?
options: After the model and tokenizer load and a small validation inference succeeds
mcq.why: Readiness means a real answer.

mcq.q: Why send warm-up requests before marking a replica ready?
options: So real users do not pay compilation and cache-allocation costs
mcq.why: Typical shapes warm the kernels and caches.

mcq.q: Cold start is 8 minutes and traffic ramps over 5 minutes. What fixes the SLO violations in the figure?
options: A larger warm pool or scheduled pre-scaling
mcq.why: Reactive scaling cannot start replicas faster than the ramp.
distractors: That sends traffic to unready replicas.

mcq.q: What conflicts with tight first-request latency targets?
mcq.why: The first request after zero pays the full cold start.

mcq.q: How should engine configuration such as TP size and max model length be managed?
options: As versioned config with a pinned engine version
Changed live in production without records
Typed by hand on each server
mcq.why: Packaging pins versions and keeps config reviewable.

mcq.why: It is the course's laptop testbed.
distractors: GPU serving engine (a slow CPU backend exists for experiments).

covers: SGLang prefix caching and structured output

mcq.q: As batch size grows, what happens to throughput and per-user latency?
options: Throughput rises then plateaus; latency keeps rising
mcq.why: Shared weight reads raise throughput until compute-bound.

mcq.q: How should the operating point be chosen?
options: By the SLO: maximise throughput subject to latency targets
mcq.why: e.g. maximise tokens/s subject to p95 ITL ≤ 50 ms.

mcq.q: What does nvidia-smi's “GPU utilisation 100%” mean?
options: A kernel was running, not that compute units were busy
All compute units were fully busy
mcq.why: Prefer tokens/s, MFU, bandwidth utilisation and KV usage.

mcq.q: Choose all admission-control measures from the chapter.
options: Reject or redirect when expected wait exceeds the deadline
mcq.why: Also prioritise interactive traffic over batch.
distractors: That lets latency grow for everyone.

mcq.q: Which vLLM setting caps concurrent sequences per replica?
mcq.why: It limits how many sequences run together.

mcq.q: Which metric suits decode efficiency?
mcq.why: Decode is bandwidth-bound; MFU suits prefill.

mcq.q: In the figure, ITL crosses 50 ms at batch 48. What batch cap should you choose?
options: Just below 48, the largest batch under the SLO
mcq.why: The best batch is the largest one under the SLO line.

mcq.q: Why keep 100k-token requests in a separate pool?
options: Long requests have no KV cache
So they cannot crowd out short chats
mcq.why: Long requests consume KV and prefill time.

mcq.q: What happens to tail latency near saturation?
mcq.why: Queues grow quickly as utilisation approaches the limit.

mcq.q: A bounded queue has an expected wait of 4 s, and an interactive request's deadline is 2 s. What should admission control do?
options: Reject or redirect the request now
Raise the batch size above the SLO
mcq.why: Rejecting early is better than missing the deadline after waiting (15.6).
distractors: That breaks the latency target for everyone.

mcq.q: Why is self-hosting cost mostly fixed?
options: You pay for GPU-hours whether or not they are busy
mcq.why: API cost is variable; self-hosting is fixed capacity.

mcq.q: Choose all the conditions under which self-hosting can win.
options: High, steady volume that keeps GPUs well used
A smaller open model meets the quality bar
mcq.why: Low, spiky traffic leaves GPUs idle.

mcq.q: 20 billion tokens a month at $0.60 per million via API costs…
One GPU at 2,500 tokens/s and 45% average utilisation delivers about how many tokens a month (about 2.63 million seconds)?
Where should the throughput input in the calculator come from?
options: Your own benchmark at your SLO with your prompt and output mix

mcq.q: Which costs belong in a self-hosted total?
options: GPUs with redundancy, engineers and on-call, networking, storage, observability and idle capacity
mcq.why: The full cost is much more than GPUs.

mcq.q: Harbor compares options by…
options: Dollars per resolved question at the same quality bar
mcq.why: A cheap token is not cheap if the task needs many calls or human fixes.

mcq.q: Why is the calculator's minimum 2 GPUs?
mcq.why: One GPU is a single point of failure.

mcq.q: What is an opportunity cost of self-hosting?
mcq.why: Hosted providers ship new models you may not be able to run.
